plan.chapterName: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 12: Static Equilibrium and Elasticity
plan.contextChunk: This figure places two panels side by side, labeled (a) and (b) beneath them, each a shaded three-dimensional cylinder standing on end and representing the same rod under opposite loading. In panel (a) a thick red arrow labeled F points straight up from above the top face and a matching red arrow labeled F points straight down from below the bottom face; a dashed outline extends above the solid cylinder to mark the stretched portion, bracketed at the left as 'Delta L', with a longer bracket below it spanning the original length 'L0'. In panel (b) the two red arrows are reversed, pressing inward from above and below, a curly leader labels the top circular face 'A', and a bracket labeled 'Delta L' at the right runs from the top face down to a dashed ellipse drawn inside the cylinder where the end formerly sat, with 'L0' bracketed at the left. Both cylinders are drawn at identical width, so the whole comparison rests on whether the dashed reference outline lies outside or inside the solid body. The pairing defines the signed length change from the undeformed length L0 that enters tensile and compressive strain, with the cross-section held constant in the low-stress linear range.

elements: single upright shaded cylinder (the rod), elliptical top and bottom faces visible
original-length reference outline: dashed cylinder/ellipse segment marking where the end face sat before loading (outside the solid body in tension, inside in compression)
red force arrow above the top face, labeled F-vector (points up/outward in tension, down/inward in compression)
red force arrow below the bottom face, labeled F-vector (points down/outward in tension, up/inward in compression)
left vertical bracket spanning the original length, labeled L0
vertical bracket for the length change, labeled ΔL (left side in tension, right side in compression)
curly leader labeling the top circular face as cross-sectional area A (visible in compression mode)
panel label beneath the figure: (a) tension or (b) compression

interactions.label: Loading mode
interactions.teaches: Reversing the loading reverses the force arrows and moves the dashed reference outline from outside to inside the cylinder, making the sign of ΔL relative to L0 explicit — tensile strain is positive, compressive strain is negative

interactions.label: Applied force F (compression ← 0 → tension)
interactions.teaches: Sweeping F through zero stretches or shortens the rod while its cross-section stays fixed, showing that in the low-stress linear range ΔL is proportional to F (via stress = F/A and Young's modulus)

demo_steps.title: Tension
demo_steps.narration: With F > 0 the arrows pull outward, the rod lengthens past L0, and the dashed outline sits above the top face — ΔL is positive, tensile strain ε = ΔL/L0 > 0.

demo_steps.title: Compression
demo_steps.narration: Switch to compression (F < 0): the arrows press inward, the rod shortens below L0, and the dashed ellipse appears inside the body — ΔL is negative. Note the cross-section A stays unchanged.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Single cylinder centered at origin, axis vertical along +Y. Radius ~0.8 world units, undeformed length L0 ~3.2 units spanning Y ∈ [-1.6, 1.6]. Deformed top face sits at Y = 1.6 + ΔL with ΔL = k·F mapped so F=±100 gives ΔL ≈ ±0.55 (≈17% of L0); radius never changes. Dashed reference: a wireframe/dashed cylinder segment (same radius) occupying the band between the original top position and the current top face — rendered as a dashed outline OUTSIDE (above) the solid in tension and as a dashed ellipse INSIDE the body in compression (its complement band shaded as part of the solid below it). Red arrows #d43a2a, thick, ~1.0 unit long shafts: top arrow tail/head arrangement flips with sign (tension: top arrow points +Y from ~0.6 above top face, bottom arrow points -Y below bottom face; compression reversed). Cylinder body: light blue-grey gradient fill (#c9d2e8 to #eef1f8) with darker outline #6a7390, top face ellipse slightly lighter. Brackets: thin dark lines with end ticks; L0 bracket on the left spanning full original length; ΔL bracket on the left in tension (matching panel a) and on the right in compression (matching panel b), spanning only the reference band. Labels L0, ΔL, F (with vector arrow), A with curly leader pointing at the top face in compression. Panel caption (a)/(b) under the cylinder updates with the mode.
interactionPlan.notes: Drive everything from the single signed F value: top-face Y position, arrow directions and lengths (scale shaft length slightly with |F|), dashed reference placement (outside vs inside), ΔL bracket side, and the A label's visibility (compression only). Keep the toggle and slider consistent — moving the slider across zero should also flip the visual mode. Draw the cylinder as a LatheGeometry or CylinderGeometry with open ends plus two ellipse discs for faces; the dashed reference can be a second wireframe cylinder segment using LineDashedMaterial. Straight-on view, no axis tilt needed beyond showing the elliptical faces.

authoredContext:
Tension or compression occurs when two antiparallel forces of equal magnitude act on an object along only one of its dimensions, in such a way that the object does not move. One way to envision such a situation is illustrated in the figure. A rod segment is either stretched or squeezed by a pair of forces acting along its length and perpendicular to its cross-section. The net effect of such forces is that the rod changes its length from the original length L0 that it had before the forces appeared, to a new length L that it has under the action of the forces. This change in length ΔL=L−L0 may be either elongation (when L is larger than the original length L0) or contraction (when L is smaller than the original length L0). Tensile stress and strain occur when the forces are stretching an object, causing its elongation, and the length change ΔL is positive. Compressive stress and strain occur when the forces are contracting an object, causing its shortening, and the length change ΔL is negative.

Compressive stress and strain are defined by the same formulas, the equation and the equation, respectively. The only difference from the tensile situation is that for compressive stress and strain, we take absolute values of the right-hand sides in the equation and the equation.

When an object is in either tension or compression, the net force on it is zero, but the object deforms by changing its original length L0. (a) Tension: The rod is elongated by ΔL. (b) Compression: The rod is contracted by ΔL. In both cases, the deforming force acts along the length of the rod and perpendicular to its cross-section. In the linear range of low stress, the cross-sectional area of the rod does not change.

Figure A is a schematic drawing of a cylinder with a length L0 that is under the tensile strain. Two forces at the different sides of cylinder increase its length by Delta L. Figure B is a schematic drawing of a cylinder with a length L0 that is under the compressive strain. Two forces at the different sides of cylinder reduce its length by Delta L.

Young’s modulus Y is the elastic modulus when deformation is caused by either tensile or compressive stress, and is defined by the equation. Dividing this equation by tensile strain, we obtain the expression for Young’s modulus:
